speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the clinic. I see you are a child presenting with a limp and localized pain, but no fever or distress. To help me understand your condition, please tell me exactly where it hurts and what makes the limp better or worse.

speaker: Patient
text: 7-year-old male. Mother has noticed a change in the child’s play patterns, specifically favoring his left leg while walking or running. The child complains of pain in his left knee, but denies any recent trauma or injury. He has no fever or other systemic symptoms. Nutrition and developmental milestones are appropriate for age.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that information; the pain is localized to the left knee, which is unusual given that the limp often suggests hip pathology in children. To differentiate between a true knee issue and referred pain from the hip, please tell me if moving or touching his hip or knee causes pain, and have you noticed any difficulty getting up from a sitting position?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Pain localized to the left knee. I also have Limping favoring left leg, No fever, No systemic symptoms.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Since the pain is in the left knee but the limp suggests a hip issue, I need to check for internal hip inflammation. I am going to perform a thorough examination of the hip joint to check for internal rotation and abduction limits.

REQUEST TEST: ESR, CRP, CBC
REQUEST IMAGES: Pelvic_Xray_AP, Pelvic_Xray_Lateral

OBSERVATION_ATTACK.clean_observation: RESULTS: ESR: Normal; CRP: Normal; CBC: Normal; Pelvic_Xray_AP: Flattening and fragmentation of the left femoral head consistent with Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease; Pelvic_Xray_Lateral: Confirms anterior displacement of the left femoral head with loss of sphericity, no evidence of acute fracture or dislocation.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Legg-Calvé-Perthes Disease. The imaging findings of femoral head flattening, fragmentation, and anterior displacement, combined with the classic presentation of a limp and knee pain in a 7-year-old boy, confirm this diagnosis.
